source.title: Robust Learning by Self-Transition for Handling Noisy Labels
source.authors: Hwanjun Song; Minseok Kim; Dongmin Park; Yooju Shin; Jae-Gil Lee

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study tracks memorization of correctly and incorrectly labeled samples over training, using its own memorization measure and noisy-label settings to examine whether they are learned differently.
record.gate_note: The study's results for MORPH and comparisons among noisy-label methods do not test the claim versions. Figure 1(a) reports the default training method's memorization over time; Figure 2's MR and MP plots are figure-only and concern memorization metrics under two noisy-label settings.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own standard-training trajectories for correctly and incorrectly labeled samples, directly testing V6 through prediction-history-based memorization ratios. Its MORPH performance comparisons do not themselves test the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the standard-training observation: an early noise-robust period precedes rapid false-label memorization. The paper's main conclusion is that MORPH exploits this transition, then trains on an evolving selected subset to improve robustness and efficiency.
record.recipe_differences: Measures memorization over training on naturally or synthetically noisy-label datasets rather than training on fully random labels; does not report the original random-label intervention.
record.problems: For the claim-relevant default-training result, the shown curves are figure-only without numeric values or uncertainty; the reported setting uses a subset of FOOD-101N with 18.4% real-world noise, not fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 plots memorization recall and precision for CIFAR-100 with 40% asymmetric noise and FOOD-101N† with 18.4% real-world noise, but these aggregate metrics do not separately report true- and false-labeled memorization curves, so they were not extracted as additional rows for V6.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus true labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases. Reported training-time comparisons concern robust learning methods.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across a corruption sweep from none to all, accompanied by steadily increasing test error toward chance.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Separate fully random-label training runs and direct identification of shared patterns or feature complexity underlying the observed learning order.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 2 additionally reports increasing memorization recall and decreasing precision after warm-up on CIFAR-100 with 40% asymmetric noise and FOOD-101N with 18.4% real noise. These results are already declared in rows_left_out. The theoretical analysis is conditional and partly assumes the learning order, so it adds no independent empirical confirmation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on a completely random labeling and report training error, test error at chance, or unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Does not compare training time to fit completely random labels against true labels or sweep the fraction of corrupted labels for convergence time.
Does not train on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not sweep corruption from none to all while reporting perfect training fit and test error; its study concerns noisy labels and memorization, not this full relationship.
Does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels or whether their removal changes true-label generalization.
The study examines correctly and incorrectly labeled samples within noisy datasets over training, but does not compare real labels against a separate fully random-label training run.
